name: The New Place Mulberry

location.address: Great Garden, Shakespeare's New Place, Chapel Street, Stratford-upon-Avon CV37 6EP

access: Paid entry to Shakespeare's New Place (Shakespeare Birthplace Trust); the tree stands in the Great Garden. Check shakespeare.org.uk for current hours and prices.
transport: Old Town, about 10 minutes' walk from Stratford-upon-Avon station.
recognise: The large, old, gnarled mulberry in New Place's Great Garden, the one that stains the lawn with fruit in late summer; a younger mulberry planted in 1969 by Dame Peggy Ashcroft stands in the same garden.
verify_notes: Owner of the ground (Shakespeare Birthplace Trust) 'Plant of the month' page for New Place: Morus nigra (Black Mulberry), location Great Garden, 'Age: believed to be around 270yrs old', believed grown from a cutting of the tree Shakespeare planted, which the Rev. Francis Gastrell felled in 1756; harvested fruit used for a New Place Mulberry Gin Liqueur; the other mulberry was planted by Dame Peggy Ashcroft in 1969. The page carries no date seen; 'around 270 years' is the Trust's own figure (so planted about 1750s-1760s, which fits a scion after the 1756 felling). SBT blog 2013 (theshakespeareblog.com/2013/08/shakespeares-mulberries/): the scion is 'a venerable and massive tree, still bearing fruit'; Ashcroft's 1969 tree split in 2013. Stratford Observer 20 Nov 2017: photo caption 'the mulberry tree which stands today in the Great Garden at New Place'. The link to Shakespeare's own tree is tradition, not proven: the Trust says 'believed'. A search-engine summary claimed an '1862 planting' for this tree; that was wrong (1862 is the year of a chair said to be made from the old tree's wood, Stratford Observer 2017). Unused. No girth or height seen. Alive: SBT fruit use and 2017 photo; no dated 2024-26 observation seen, so recent life not independently confirmed.
story:
Shakespeare's own mulberry was cut down in 1756, and this one may be its child. The Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, which looks after the site of his last home at New Place, believes the black mulberry in the Great Garden grew from a cutting of the tree the poet is said to have planted, felled that year by the Reverend Francis Gastrell. Both halves of that sentence are tradition. The Trust says believed, and so do we.

The Trust puts the tree at around 270 years old, which fits a cutting taken soon after the felling. Its blog called it, in 2013, a venerable and massive tree still bearing fruit, and it still earns its keep. The Trust harvests the mulberries for a New Place Mulberry Gin Liqueur.

The felled tree did not disappear either. Its wood became souvenirs, among them a chair dated 1862 that is said to have been made from it. One tradition ended up as furniture, the other is still growing in the garden where it began.

A second, younger mulberry shares the garden, planted by the actor Dame Peggy Ashcroft in 1969. It split in 2013. New Place is ticketed and about ten minutes on foot from Stratford-upon-Avon station.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the larger, older of the two mulberries in the Great Garden, a massive trunk that still bears fruit. The younger one nearby was planted by Dame Peggy Ashcroft in 1969.

best_time.label: July and August, when the dark mulberries ripen and the Trust harvests them

name: The Hall's Croft Mulberry

location.address: Hall's Croft garden, Old Town, Stratford-upon-Avon CV37 6BG

access: Paid entry to Hall's Croft (Shakespeare Birthplace Trust); check shakespeare.org.uk for current hours and prices.
transport: Old Town, about 12 minutes' walk from Stratford-upon-Avon station, near Holy Trinity Church.
recognise: A mulberry whose trunk grows almost horizontally across a flower bed in the Hall's Croft garden, held up on supports.
verify_notes: Single source, the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust's Shakespeare Blog (2013): the mulberry at Hall's Croft 'appears to be growing horizontally among a bed of flowers' and, once supported, will take on the character of the older New Place trees; the same post notes the RHS advice that old mulberries lean and split. The post does not give species (assumed Morus nigra, as at New Place, not stated for this tree), age, girth or exact position. Alive: 2013 only, no later observation seen. Flagged: one source, species assumed, no recent life check. Owner of the ground is the source. Pin is the garden, approximate.
story:
The mulberry at Hall's Croft grows sideways. Its trunk runs almost horizontally through a bed of flowers in the garden of the house where Shakespeare's daughter Susanna lived with her husband, the physician John Hall. The Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, which owns the house, wrote in 2013 that once supported it would take on the character of the much older mulberries at New Place.

Leaning is what old mulberries do. The same post quotes the Royal Horticultural Society's advice that they lean and split with age. Whether this one has since been given its supports, nobody has published.

That 2013 post is the only account of the tree we have found. It does not give its age, its girth or even its species, though black mulberry, the kind at New Place, is the likely answer. Nobody has dated it. If you visit, tell us what you find, how far it leans now, and whether it fruits.

It shares the town with the New Place mulberry, which the Trust believes grew from a cutting of Shakespeare's own, a short walk away through the Old Town. Hall's Croft is ticketed, near Holy Trinity Church, about twelve minutes on foot from the station.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk running almost horizontally across a flower bed. It stands in the garden of Hall's Croft, near Holy Trinity Church.
